title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 71 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 448–450 (Night 71, continuing directly from nights-70), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 71 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Ḍawʾ al-Makān, travelling toward Baghdad with the caravan and the stoker, remembers his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān and recites verses of longing; in Baghdad she, sleepless the same night, hears her brother’s voice carried to her, and sends the eunuch to fetch the singer — and the night ends as he answers that he has not heard him. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.l: And when it was the night, the one-and-the-seventy,
sentences.i: And when it was the seventy-first night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُمْ أَقَامُوا فِي مَدِينَةِ حَمَاةَ ثَلْثَةَ أَيَّامٍ ثُمَّ سَافَرُوا وَمَا زَالُوا مُسَافِرِينَ حَتَّى وَصَلُوا إِلَي مَدِينَةٍ أُخْرَى
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahum aqāmū fī madīnati Ḥamāta thalthata ayyāmin thumma sāfarū wa-mā zālū musāfirīna ḥattā waṣalū ilā madīnatin ukhrā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that they stayed in the city of Ḥamāh three days, then travelled, and they did not cease travelling until they reached another city.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that they stayed three days in the city of Ḥamāh, then travelled on, and went on travelling until they came to another city.
sentences.n: ثلثة is the edition’s spelling of ثلاثة, “three” (the alif of the long vowel is not written); kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَأَقَامُوا بِهَا ثَلْثَةَ أَيَّامٍ ثُمَّ سَافَرُوا حَتَّى دَخَلُوا دِيَارَ بَكْرٍ وَهَبَّ عَلَيْهِمْ نَسِيمُ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-aqāmū bi-hā thalthata ayyāmin thumma sāfarū ḥattā dakhalū diyāra Bakrin wa-habba ʿalayhim nasīmu Baghdāda
sentences.l: And they stayed in it three days, then travelled until they entered the abodes of Bakr, and there blew on them the breeze of Baghdad.
sentences.i: They stayed there three days, then travelled on until they entered Diyār Bakr, and a breeze from Baghdad blew over them.
sentences.n: ديار بكر (Diyār Bakr) is the upper-Tigris country, “the lands of the tribe of Bakr”. Here بها is “in it”, bi- marking the place where they stayed.

sentences.t: فَتَذَكَّرَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ أُخْتَهُ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ وَأَبَاهُ وَأُمَّهُ وَوَطَنَهُ وَكَيْفَ يَرْجِعُ إِلَي أَبِيهِ بِغَيْرِ أُخْتِهِ فَبَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَاشْتَدَّتْ بِهِ الْحَسَرَاتُ
sentences.tr: fa-tadhakkara Ḍawʾu al-Makāni ukhtahu Nuzhata al-Zamāni wa-abāhu wa-ummahu wa-waṭanahu wa-kayfa yarjiʿu ilā abīhi bi-ghayri ukhtihi fa-bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-ishtaddat bihi al-ḥasarātu
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān remembered his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān, and his father, and his mother, and his homeland, and how he would return to his father without his sister; and he wept, and groaned, and complained, and the regrets grew intense with him.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān remembered his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān, and his father and mother and his homeland, and how he could go back to his father without his sister; and he wept and groaned and made his complaint, and his sorrows grew ever sharper.
sentences.n: The name is “Light of the Place”; Nuzhat al-Zamān is “Delight of the Age”.

sentences.l: And he recited, saying these verses —
sentences.n: The print breaks the last word with dashes (الاب—ي—ات); it is read as الأبيات, “the verses”.

sentences.t:
خَلِيلَيَ كَمْ هَذَا التأنِّي وَاصْبِرُ * وَلَمْ يَأْتِنِي مِنكُمْ رَسُولْ يُخْبِرُ
الَا إِنَّ أَيَّامَ الْوِصَالِ قَصِيرَةُ * فَيَا لَيْتَ أَيَّامَ التفرُّقِ تَقصُرُ
خُذُوا بِيَدِيْ ثُمَّ اكْشِفُوا الثَّوْبَ تَنْظُرُوا * ضَنَىْ جَسَدِيْ لَكِنَّنِي اتَسَتَّرُ
وَإِنْ قَالَ لِيْ أَسْلُوا هَوَاكُمْ اقُلْ لَهُ * فَوَاللهِ مَا اسْلُوا لِيْ حِيْنَ احْشَرُ
sentences.tr:
khalīlayya kam hādhā al-taʾannī wa-aṣbiru * wa-lam yaʾtinī minkum rasūlun yukhbiru
alā inna ayyāma al-wiṣāli qaṣīratun * fa-yā layta ayyāma al-tafarruqi taqṣuru
khudhū bi-yadī thumma ikshifū al-thawba tanẓurū * ḍanā jasadī lakinnanī atasattaru
wa-in qāla lī aslū hawākum aqul lahu * fa-wa-allāhi mā aslū lī ḥīna aḥsharu
sentences.l:
O my two friends, how-much (is) this forbearance, and I am patient — and there has not come to me from you a messenger who informs.
Ah — the days of union are short; and oh, would that the days of parting were short.
Take by my hand, then uncover the garment, you will see the wasting of my body — but I hide myself.
And if one says to me, “Forget your love,” I say to him: By God, I shall not forget, to me, when I am mustered.
sentences.i:
My two friends, how long must this waiting go on, while I endure it, and no messenger has come to me from you with news?
The days of union are short, and would that the days of parting were short too.
Take my hand and lift away the garment, and you will see how my body has wasted — though I keep myself hidden.
And if anyone tells me, “Forget your love,” I tell him: By God, I shall not forget it even on the day I am raised up.
sentences.n: Verse copied exactly as the edition prints it, marks and all, including its odd forms: اتَسَتَّرُ is read as a-tasattaru, “I conceal myself” (a verb of the fifth form); لِيْ in the last line is a pleonastic “to me”; and “when I am mustered” (ḥīna uḥsharu) means the Day of Resurrection.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَقَّادُ اتْرُكْ هَذَا الْبُكَاءَ وَالْأَنِينَ فَإِنَّنَا قَرِيبٌ مِنْ خَيْمَةِ الْحَاجِبِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-waqqādu utruk hādhā al-bukāʾa wa-al-anīna fa-innanā qarībun min khaymati al-ḥājibi
sentences.l: And the stoker said to him: Leave this weeping and the groaning, for we are near to the tent of the chamberlain.
sentences.i: The stoker said to him: Stop this weeping and groaning, for we are close to the chamberlain’s tent.
sentences.n: The print has the singular قريب (“near”) after “we”; kept as printed — a common Middle Arabic agreement.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ لَابُدَّ مِنْ إِنْشَادِي شَيْأً مِنَ الشِّعْرِ لَعَلَّ نَارَ قَلْبِي تَنْطَفِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Ḍawʾu al-Makāni lā budda min inshādī shayʾan mina al-shiʿri laʿalla nāra qalbī tanṭafī
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: There is no escape from my reciting something of poetry; perhaps the fire of my heart will go out.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: I must recite a little poetry; perhaps the fire in my heart will die down.
sentences.n: The print runs لا بد together (لابد) and writes “something” as شياً (shayʾan, without the hamza-seat); both are kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَقَّادُ بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ اتْرُكِ الْحُزْنَ حَتَّى تَصِلَ إِلَى بِلَادِكَ وَافْعَلْ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ مَا شِئْتَ وَأَنَا مَعَكَ حَيْثُ مَاكُنْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-waqqādu bi-allāhi ʿalayka utruki al-ḥuzna ḥattā taṣila ilā bilādika wa-afʿal baʿda dhālika mā shiʾta wa-anā maʿaka ḥaythu mā kunta
sentences.l: And the stoker said to him: By God upon you, leave the grief until you arrive at your country, and do after that what you will; and I am with you wherever you were.
sentences.i: The stoker said to him: For God’s sake, put your grief aside until you reach your own country, and after that do as you please; I will be with you wherever you are.
sentences.n: بالله عليك is an oath-plea, “by God, [I adjure] you”. The print runs ما كنت together (ماكنت), “wherever you may be”; kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ وَاللَّهِ لَا أَفْتُرُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Ḍawʾu al-Makāni wa-allāhi lā aftur ʿan dhālika
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: By God, I will not slacken from that.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: By God, I will not give it up.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ بِوَجْهِهِ إِلَى نَاحِيَةِ بَغْدَادَ وَكَانَ الْقَمَرُ مُضِئاً مُسْبِلًا أَنْوَارَهُ وَنُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ لَمْ تَنَمْ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ فَقَلِقَتْ وَتَذَكَّرَتْ أَخَاهَا ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ وَبَكَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata bi-wajhihi ilā nāḥiyati Baghdāda wa-kāna al-qamaru muḍīʾan musbilan anwārahu wa-Nuzhatu al-Zamāni lam tanam tilka al-laylata fa-qaliqat wa-tadhakkarat akhāhā Ḍawʾa al-Makāni wa-bakat
sentences.l: Then he turned with his face toward the direction of Baghdad; and the moon was shining, letting down its lights; and Nuzhat al-Zamān had not slept that night, and was restless, and remembered her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and wept.
sentences.i: Then he turned his face toward Baghdad. The moon was bright and shed its light far and wide. Nuzhat al-Zamān had not slept that night; she was restless, and she thought of her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and wept.
sentences.n: The print spells “shining” مضياً (muḍīʾan) without the hamza-seat; kept as printed. The scene is the same night in two places: his tent near Diyār Bakr, her chamber in Baghdad.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هِيَ تَبْكِى إِذْ سَمِعَتْ أَخَاهَا ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ يَبْكِى وَهُوَ يُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā hiya tabkī idh samiʿat akhāhā Ḍawʾa al-Makāni yabkī wa-huwa yunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: And while she was weeping, behold, she heard her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān weeping, and he was reciting these verses — poetry.
sentences.i: While she was weeping, she heard her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān weeping too, and reciting these verses:
sentences.n: The print writes the ending of تبكى and يبكى with a dotless ى; kept as printed. The final شعر (“poetry”) is the edition’s heading for the verses that follow.

sentences.t:
لَمَعَ الْبَرْقُ الْيَمَانِيْ * فَشَجَانِيْْ مَا شَجَانِي
مِنْ حَبِيبٍ كَانَ عِنْدِيْ * سَاقِيًا كَأْسَ التَّهَانِيْ
ذَكَّرَنِيْ مَنْ قَدْ رَمَانِيْْ * بِالْحِمَى لَمَّا رَمَانِي
يَا وَمِيضَ الْبَرْقِ هَلْ * تَرْجِعُ اَيَّامُ التَّدَانِيْ
يَا عَذُوْلِيْ لَا تَلُمْنِيْ * إِنَّ رَبِّيْ قَدْ بَلَانِيْ
بِحَبِيبٍ غَابَ عَنِّيْ * وَزَمَانٍ قَدْ دَهَانِيْ
قَدْ نَأَتْ نُزْهَةُ قَلْبِيْ * عِنْدَ مَا وَلَّى زَمَانِيْ
وَحُوى لِيَ الْهَمَّ صِرْفًا * وَبِكَأْسٍ قَدْ سَقَانِيْ
وَاَرَانِيْ يَا خَلِيْلِيْ * مَيِّتٌ قَبْلَ التَّدَانِيْ
يَا زَمَانِيْ بِالتَّصَابِيْ * عُدْ قَرِيبًا بِالتَّهَانِيْ
فِي سُرُوْرٍ مَعَ اَمَانٍ * مِنْ سَهْمِ هَمٍّ قَدْ رَمَانِيْ
مَنْ لِمِسْكِيْنٍ غَرِيبٍ * بَاتَ مَرْعُوْبَ الْجَنَانِ
ظَلَّ فِى الْحُزْنِ فَرِيدًا * بَعْدَ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ
حَكَّمَتْ فِينَا بِرَغْمِ * كَفِّ اَوْلَادِ الزَّوَانِيْ
sentences.tr:
lamaʿa al-barqu al-yamānī * fa-shajānī mā shajānī
min ḥabībin kāna ʿindī * sāqiyan kaʾsa al-tahānī
dhakkaranī man qad ramānī * bi-al-ḥimā lammā ramānī
yā wamīḍa al-barqi hal * tarjiʿu ayyāmu al-tadānī
yā ʿadhūlī lā talumnī * inna rabbī qad balānī
bi-ḥabībin ghāba ʿannī * wa-zamānin qad dahānī
qad naʾat nuzhatu qalbī * ʿinda mā wallā zamānī
wa-ḥuwā lī al-hamma ṣirfan * wa-bi-kaʾsin qad saqānī
wa-arānī yā khalīlī * mayyitun qabla al-tadānī
yā zamānī bi-al-taṣābī * ʿud qarīban bi-al-tahānī
fī surūrin maʿa amānin * min sahmi hammin qad ramānī
man li-miskīnin gharībin * bāta marʿūba al-janāni
ẓalla fī al-ḥuzni farīdan * baʿda nuzhati al-zamāni
ḥakkamat fīnā bi-raghmi * kaffi awlādi al-zawānī
sentences.l:
The Yemeni lightning flashed, and it grieved me, what grieved me,
from a beloved who was with me, pouring the cup of felicitations;
it reminded me of him who has shot me, in the sacred-pasture, when he shot me.
O flash of the lightning, will the days of nearness return?
O my blamer, do not blame me, my Lord has tried me
with a beloved who is gone from me, and a time that has afflicted me.
The delight of my heart has gone far, when my time turned away,
and it gathered for me grief unmixed, and with a cup [it] gave me to drink,
and it showed me, O my friend, dead before the nearness.
O my time of youthful folly, return soon with felicitations,
in joy, with safety from the arrow of a grief that has shot me.
Who is there for a poor stranger who spent the night with the heart terrified,
remaining in sorrow alone after the Delight of the Age?
She ruled over us, in spite of — the hand of the sons of whores.
sentences.i:
The lightning of Yemen flashed, and it stirred in me what it stirred,
the memory of a beloved who was once beside me, pouring the cup of happiness.
It reminded me of the one who wounded me at the sacred pasture, when he wounded me.
O glimmer of the lightning, will the days of closeness ever come back?
O you who blame me, do not blame me; my Lord has tried me
with a beloved who is gone from me, and a time that has struck me down.
The delight of my heart has gone far away, now that my days have turned,
and it has gathered grief for me, pure and unmixed, and given me a cup to drink,
and shown me, my friend, that I am a dead man before we meet again.
O time of my youthful follies, come back soon with happiness,
in joy and safety from the arrow of grief that has struck me.
Who will take pity on a poor stranger who spends the night with a terrified heart,
left alone in his sorrow now that Nuzhat al-Zamān is gone?
Fate has ruled over us in despite of — the hand of the sons of whores.
sentences.n: The print has قل (6 times), a misprint for قد, corrected here. Otherwise the verse is copied exactly as the edition prints it, marks and all. وَحُوى (line 8) is printed with a damma on the ḥāʾ and read as ḥawā, “gathered”; and the closing line, whose first words seem to speak of fate, is obscure. نُزْهَةُ قَلْبِي (line 7) plays on the name of Nuzhat al-Zamān, which comes back openly in line 13.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ صَاحَ وَخَرَّ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ، هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi ṣāḥa wa-kharra maghshiyyan ʿalayhi, hādhā mā kāna min amrihi
sentences.l: And when he finished with his poetry he cried out and fell fainting upon himself — this is what was of his affair.
sentences.i: When he had finished his poem he cried out and fell down in a faint. So much for him.
sentences.n: The print puts the comma after عليه; kept as printed. هذا ما كان من أمره is the storyteller’s stock “so much for him”, before turning to the other party.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ فَإِنَّهَا كَانَتْ سَاهِرَةً فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ لِأَنَّهَا تَذَكَّرَتْ أَخَاهَا فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ ذَلِكَ الصَّوْتَ بِاللَّيْلِ ارْتَاحَ فُؤَادُهَا وَقَامَتْ وَتَبَحْبَحَتْ وَدَعَتِ الْخَادِمَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri Nuzhati al-Zamāni fa-innahā kānat sāhiratan fī tilka al-laylati li-annahā tadhakkarat akhāhā fī dhālika al-makāni fa-lammā samiʿat dhālika al-ṣawta bi-al-layli irtāḥa fuʾāduhā wa-qāmat wa-tabaḥbaḥat wa-daʿati al-khādima
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of Nuzhat al-Zamān, she was wakeful on that night, because she had remembered her brother in that place; and when she heard that voice in the night, her heart was eased, and she rose, and settled-herself-at-ease, and called the servant.
sentences.i: As for Nuzhat al-Zamān, she was lying awake that night because she had been thinking of her brother in that place; and when she heard that voice in the night her heart stirred with relief. She got up, sat herself upright, and called the eunuch.
sentences.n: تبحبحت (tabaḥbaḥat) is read as “she settled herself, took her ease”; its sense here is a little uncertain — she is sitting up or shifting to listen. الخادم, “the servant”, is the palace eunuch.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَا حَاجَتُكِ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ قُمْ وَائْتِنِي بِهَذَا الَّذِي يُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَشْعَارَ فَقَالَ لَهَا الْخَادِمُ إِنِّي لَمْ أَسْمَعْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā mā ḥājatuki fa-qālat lahu qum wa-ʾtinī bi-hādhā allādhī yunshidu hādhihi al-ashʿāra fa-qāla lahā al-khādimu innī lam asmaʿhu
sentences.l: And he said to her: What is your need? And she said to him: Rise, and bring me this one who recites these poems. And the servant said to her: Indeed, I did not hear him,
sentences.i: He said to her: What do you need? She said: Get up and bring me the man who is reciting these poems. But the servant said to her: I did not hear him —
sentences.n: The edition prints the verb وائتني with its hamza-seat already (wa-iʾtinī, “and bring me”); kept as printed. The servant’s reply breaks off at the night’s close, as the formula takes over.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَ—احِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The stock close of a night. The print’s last word is damaged (المب—اح, with a dash inside it); it is read as the formula’s usual al-mubāḥ.
